description: GUARD — GPU-native drift and anomaly monitoring for ML inference. Drift signals, per-detector detail, and the monitor's own health. Thresholds shown here are placeholders; calibrate them per model against your own clean traffic (see deploy/grafana/README.md).

panels.title: Mean output entropy
panels.description:
Rolling-window mean Shannon entropy (nats) of the model's softmax output, averaged over the last `window_size` steps.

**Healthy:** a flat, narrow band at whatever level your clean traffic settles on. 0 = a fully confident model, ln(C) = uniform guessing (for C classes).

**Unhealthy:** a sustained climb is confidence collapse — the model is hedging on inputs it no longer recognises. A sustained drop toward 0 usually means a degenerate head (everything mapped to one class), not improved accuracy.

The absolute level is model-specific and carries no meaning across models; judge the shape against this deployment's own history.

panels.title: JS divergence vs baseline class mix
panels.description:
Jensen-Shannon divergence between the live predicted-class distribution and the baseline's. Symmetric and bounded in [0, ln 2] = 0.693, which is why it is the preferred alerting signal — a threshold set here means the same thing on any model.

**Healthy:** small and noisy around a constant floor. The floor is never exactly 0: a finite window over a finite class set always carries sampling noise, and smaller windows raise the floor.

**Unhealthy:** a step change or a monotone rise = prior/label shift, the predicted class mix moving away from calibration. Values approaching 0.693 mean the live and baseline distributions have almost disjoint support.

panels.title: Active drift alerts
panels.description:
Number of detectors whose change-point test is currently latched in alarm, from `guard_drift_alert{detector}`.

**Healthy:** 0. **Unhealthy:** anything above 0 — check which detector in the panels below, then the alert payload (detector, metric, value, statistic, threshold, model and baseline version) in your alert sink.

The gauge latches for `alert_hold` windows after a firing and clears on its own once the stream is quiet, so a brief spike stays visible for at least one scrape and a genuine recovery does not need a manual reset.

Caveat: `guard_drift_alert` has no series at all until the first alert state transition in a process, which is why this query falls back to `vector(0)` — a reading of 0 here means either 'no alert' or 'no alert yet'. Cross-check `guard_steps_observed_total` in the bottom row to confirm GUARD is actually seeing traffic.

panels.title: Embedding Mahalanobis distance (per-sample mean)
panels.description:
Batch-mean Mahalanobis distance from the penultimate embeddings to the baseline Gaussian (a distance, not a squared distance).

**Healthy:** roughly constant. For a D-dimensional embedding that genuinely matches the reference Gaussian the mean sits near sqrt(D) — about 27.7 for D = 768 — so a large-looking number is normal and only the *change* matters.

**Unhealthy:** a sustained rise = covariate shift. This is the earliest signal for the failure mode where inputs come from a new regime (new camera, new season, new user cohort) and the model keeps emitting confident, wrong predictions.

panels.title: Embedding mean shift
panels.description:
Mahalanobis distance of the *running* embedding mean to the reference mean. Averaging first and measuring second cancels per-sample noise, so this is far more sensitive to a small systematic displacement than the per-sample panel — and far less reactive to a handful of genuine outliers.

**Healthy:** near 0 and drifting slowly within a narrow band.

**Unhealthy:** a clear rise away from 0 = the whole population has moved, not just a few samples. The running statistics forget exponentially (~100-batch memory by default), so this must come back down within a few hundred batches after traffic recovers; if it does not, the shift is still present.

panels.title: KL divergence vs baseline class mix
panels.description:
KL(P||Q) between the live and baseline predicted-class distributions.

**Healthy:** small and stable. **Unhealthy:** rising, same story as JS.

Diagnostic rather than alerting: KL is asymmetric and unbounded, so a class the baseline barely saw can dominate it and no fixed threshold transfers between models. Alert on JS; read KL to understand the magnitude and direction of the prior shift.

panels.title: Entropy tail quantile
panels.description:
The configured tail quantile (`detectors.entropy.params.quantile`, default 0.99) of per-sample entropy. The tail moves before the mean does: a small cohort of unrecognisable inputs lifts this panel while 'Mean output entropy' still looks flat.

**Healthy:** stable, sitting above the mean by a constant gap.

**Unhealthy:** the gap to the mean widening = a growing minority of confused predictions.

This gauge always carries the true configured quantile. `guard_entropy_p99` is a separate gauge fed only when the configured quantile really is 0.99, which is why this dashboard plots the generic one.

panels.title: Entropy population shift (TV distance)
panels.description:
Total-variation distance between the live entropy histogram and the baseline's, binned on the baseline's own edges. Bounded in [0, 1].

**Healthy:** low and flat. Small windows keep it off zero; that floor is sampling noise, not drift.

**Unhealthy:** a rise toward 1 = the *shape* of the confidence distribution changed, not just its mean. Catches bimodal failures the mean hides — e.g. half the traffic becoming more confident while the other half collapses.

panels.title: Embedding covariance drift
panels.description:
||Sigma_run * Sigma_ref^-1 - I||_F: how far the live embedding covariance has rotated or rescaled relative to the reference. 0 means identical second-order structure.

**Healthy:** a low plateau. **Unhealthy:** growth, especially with a flat mean shift — the population has not moved but its *shape* has, which is the signature of a shift in input diversity (a new sub-population, or a collapse to a narrower one).

Recomputed every `cov_every` steps (O(D^3), comparable to a whole transformer layer at D = 768), so this line is a staircase, not a curve. If the metric is absent, `cov_every` is 0 and the detector does not emit it.

panels.title: observe() overhead on the inference thread
panels.description:
EMA (~100 steps) of the CPU microseconds `observe()` adds to the serving thread — enqueue cost only, since the detectors run on the monitor stream and nothing on this path reads a value back from the device.

**Healthy:** a low, flat line, small relative to your inference step time.

**Unhealthy:** a rise, or a step change after a deploy. A jump into the hundreds-of-microseconds range usually means something reintroduced a host synchronisation (`.item()`, `.cpu()`, printing a CUDA tensor) into the hot path — at which point the monitor is no longer free.

The threshold line is a PLACEHOLDER: 200 us = 2% of a 10 ms inference step. Replace it with 2% of your own measured step time; the < 2% p99 target is an SLO to verify on hardware, not a value this dashboard can assume.

panels.title: Ring buffer utilisation
panels.description:
Fraction of on-GPU ring slots whose monitor work has not finished yet, sampled with a non-blocking event query.

**Healthy:** low and bouncing — the monitor stream keeps up and drains slots as fast as inference fills them.

**Unhealthy:** persistently near 1.0 = the monitor stream is falling behind inference. Detection lag grows, and monitor kernels start competing for SMs instead of filling gaps. Fixes, in order: raise `drain_every_k`, raise `window_size`, raise the embedding detector's `cov_every`, or drop a detector.

panels.title: Steps observed /s
panels.description:
Batches successfully enqueued onto the monitor stream, per second. This is the liveness signal for the whole dashboard.

**Healthy:** tracks your serving throughput.

**Unhealthy:** 0 while traffic is flowing = GUARD is not seeing it. Check the global kill-switch (`enabled: false` in config, or `GUARD_DISABLED=1` in the environment), that the engine breaker has not tripped, and the dropped-batches panel to the left. Every other panel on this dashboard is meaningless while this one is flat at 0.

panels.title: Detector failures /s
panels.description:
Rate of detector exceptions caught by the GUARD safety firewall, broken out by `detector` (`guard_detector_failures_total{detector}`). The firewall swallows the exception so it never reaches the serving path, so this counter is the only early warning that a detector is misbehaving.

**Healthy:** flat at 0.

**Unhealthy:** any sustained non-zero rate. After `max_detector_failures` (default 3) the breaker trips, the detector is disabled for good, and the panel to the right goes above 0 — at which point this rate falls back to 0 because the detector is no longer being called. A burst here followed by silence is the signature of a tripped breaker, not of a recovery.

Common causes: a baseline whose `num_classes`/`embed_dim` no longer match the model, a singular covariance in the embedding detector, or a dtype the detector math cannot handle. The traceback is logged once per failure under the `guard.safety` logger.

panels.title: Detectors disabled by circuit breaker
panels.description:
Detectors the safety firewall has switched off after repeated exceptions (`max_detector_failures`, default 3). Inference is untouched either way — that is the point of the firewall — but a disabled detector is a blind spot.

**Healthy:** 0. **Unhealthy:** anything above 0. Correlate with `guard_detector_failures_total{detector}` to see which one, and check the `guard.safety` logs for the traceback. A disabled detector's metrics simply stop updating; the drift panels above will look deceptively calm.

panels.title: Summaries dropped /s
panels.description:
Rate of scalar summaries dropped because every pinned host buffer was still in flight — export backpressure. GUARD drops and counts rather than buffering without bound, so inference is never held up by a slow drain.

**Healthy:** flat 0.

**Unhealthy:** anything sustained above 0 = your dashboards have gaps and drift may go unseen. Usually the drain thread is starved (a busy GIL) or `max_pending_drains` is too small for the configured `drain_every_k`. Occasional single spikes during startup or a load burst are tolerable.

panels.title: Observations dropped /s
panels.description:
Rate of batches `observe()` rejected outright: wrong rank or width, wrong device, batch larger than `max_batch`, or an active CUDA graph capture.

**Healthy:** flat 0.

**Unhealthy:** a constant non-zero rate means GUARD is wired up wrong and is monitoring nothing — a misshaped call repeats every single step. Only the first rejection is logged with a reason; find it in the serving logs at WARNING level. A rate that tracks a specific batch size points at `max_batch`.
